title: Nutrient runoff investigation
context: A pond receives runoff from several fields. A researcher proposes testing vegetated buffers using independent replicated field plots.
prompts: State a testable hypothesis linking buffers to phosphorus loading.
Identify independent and dependent variables.
Describe a suitable control and one confounder.
Explain the nutrient-to-oxygen mechanism being investigated.
criteria: Predict buffer plots will have lower phosphorus mass in runoff under comparable events.
Independent variable: buffer treatment; response: phosphorus load, measured using both concentration and volume.
Use randomly assigned comparable unbuffered plots; control slope, rainfall and fertilizer input.
Nutrient stimulation of biomass followed by respiration and decomposition can deplete oxygen; nutrients do not simply consume it directly.

title: Diversity after disturbance
context: Before disturbance, a site has counts 10, 10, 10 and 10 for four species. Later it has 34, 2, 2 and 2. Total abundance is unchanged.
prompts: Compare richness.
Compare evenness.
Explain why these data alone do not establish the cause.
Propose a design to test a management action.
criteria: Richness remains four.
Evenness falls as one species dominates.
Other site conditions, sampling and time effects could differ; before-after association alone is insufficient.
Use replicated comparable treatment and control plots, consistent sampling and a defined ecological response.

title: Population calculations
context: A population has crude birth rate 25 and death rate 10 per thousand. Assume no migration and constant rates only for the calculation.
prompts: Calculate natural increase as a percentage.
Estimate doubling time.
Explain how migration would enter total growth.
Explain why the estimate is not a reliable fixed long-run prediction.
criteria: Rule-of-70 estimate is 70 / 1.5 ≈ 46.7 years.
Add immigration and subtract emigration in the population balance.
Fertility, mortality, age structure and resources can change; constant exponential growth is an assumption.

title: A watershed storm budget
context: A 20 mm storm falls on a 10000 m² site. Assume runoff coefficient 0.6 before a design change and 0.4 after, with the same storm and area.
prompts: Convert depth and calculate rainfall volume.
Calculate runoff before and after.
Calculate percent runoff reduction.
Explain a model limitation and a field measurement needed.
criteria: 20 mm = 0.02 m; rainfall volume = 200 m³.
Before 120 m³; after 80 m³.
A constant coefficient omits soil saturation and timing; measure actual event runoff under comparable conditions.

title: Irrigation improvement
context: A farm supplies 600 m³ of useful crop water with withdrawals of 1000 m³. A proposed system supplies the same amount using 750 m³.
prompts: Calculate efficiency before and after.
Calculate withdrawal savings.
Explain why basin savings could differ.
Name one soil or crop outcome to monitor.
criteria: Before 60%; after 80%.
Withdrawals fall by 250 m³, or 25%.
Changed return flows or expanded irrigated area can change basin-wide results.
Monitor soil salinity, crop yield or another justified indicator with consistent methods.

title: Comparing electricity services
context: A device uses 2 kW for 5 hours daily. A replacement provides the same service at 1.2 kW for the same time. Evaluate only operating electricity here.
prompts: Calculate daily energy use for both.
Calculate daily and 30-day savings.
Calculate percent operating-energy reduction.
Identify one impact excluded from this boundary.
criteria: Before 10 kWh/day; after 6 kWh/day.
Savings are 4 kWh/day and 120 kWh over 30 days.
Manufacturing, disposal, upstream generation and changes in use are excluded; do not call the operating calculation a full life-cycle result.

title: An emissions-control test
context: A plant’s measured particulate mass flow falls from 100 to 15 kg/day after a filter is installed. Production rate is held constant during comparable tests.
prompts: Calculate removal efficiency.
Distinguish particulate control from CO2 control.
Describe one design feature strengthening the comparison.
Name a residual management issue.
criteria: Removal is 85%.
A particle filter does not automatically remove gaseous CO2.
Use repeated comparable inlet/outlet tests, instrument calibration and control of operating conditions.
Captured waste needs handling and disposal; verify maintenance and actual long-term performance.

title: Treatment and loading
context: Wastewater enters at 200 mg/L of an organic-demand indicator and leaves at 40 mg/L. Flow is 100000 L/day at both locations for this calculation.
prompts: Calculate concentration-removal efficiency.
Calculate daily incoming and outgoing indicator mass in kg.
Explain one downstream oxygen implication.
Explain what this indicator does not establish.
criteria: Removal is 80%.
Incoming 20 kg/day; outgoing 4 kg/day, using 1000000 mg per kg.
Lower biodegradable organic loading can reduce downstream oxygen consumption during decomposition.
This result alone does not establish removal of all pathogens, nutrients or toxicants.

title: Testing habitat management
context: A treated site’s focal population rises from 100 to 130; an untreated site rises from 100 to 120 over the same period.
prompts: Calculate each percent change.
Explain why treated-site improvement alone does not prove effectiveness.
Propose a stronger design.
Name one tradeoff or additional response to monitor.
criteria: Treated +30%; untreated +20%.
A background trend or site difference could contribute; do not attribute the full increase to treatment.
Use replicated comparable sites, random assignment where feasible and consistent repeated sampling.
Monitor effects on other species, habitat quality, cost or another justified unintended outcome.
